symptoms: Ringspots and mottling on leaves and fruit
Chlorotic blotches and line patterns on leaves

mechanism: Acquisition occurs only in larval stage (1st and early 2nd instar)
Virus circulates and multiplies in vector's gut and salivary glands
Adult thrips remain infective for life but do not transmit to offspring
Transmission can occur in 5–10 minutes of feeding

life_cycle.TSWV_infection_duration: lifelong in vector acquired as larva

economic_impact: Serious losses in vegetables, field crops, and ornamentals
Considered one of the most economically devastating plant viruses globally

prevention: Remove infected plants and old crops
Maintain weed-free buffers of at least 25 m
Sanitation practices in greenhouses and fields
resistant_varieties: Use TSWV-resistant capsicum and tomato varieties
Consider resistance-breaking strains and maintain hygiene
chemical_control: Limited value of insecticides against vectors due to rapid resistance
Insecticides may reduce thrips populations but do not eliminate virus spread
biological_control: Predators of thrips such as Orius insidiosus (minute pirate bugs) and Geocoris punctipes (big-eyed bugs)

notes: Virus spreads only via thrips, not by seed, other insects, handling, or soil
TSWV has a very wide host range (>900 species in Australia alone)
Other related tospoviruses include CaCV, INSV, IYSV
